reference.source: GeneReviews / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Lafora disease is a severe autosomal recessive progressive myoclonic epilepsy caused by biallelic variants in EPM2A (laforin) or NHLRC1 (malin)
It typically begins in previously healthy adolescents with myoclonus, occipital and generalised seizures including visual seizures, and progressive cognitive decline
The hallmark is relentless deterioration into dementia, worsening intractable myoclonus, and dependency, unlike the milder course of Unverricht-Lundborg disease
Diagnosis is confirmed by molecular genetic testing; historically periodic acid-Schiff-positive Lafora bodies (polyglucosan inclusions) are demonstrated in skin (eccrine duct) or other tissues
EEG shows progressive background slowing with generalised and occipital epileptiform discharges and photosensitivity
Treatment is symptomatic with anti-myoclonic and antiseizure medication; sodium-channel-blocking agents can worsen myoclonus and should generally be avoided
Genetic counselling and early palliative planning are important given the poor prognosis
reference.pathophysiology: Lafora disease results from defective regulation of glycogen synthesis. Laforin (a glycogen phosphatase) and malin (an E3 ubiquitin ligase) normally act together to control glycogen branching and chain length. Loss of either protein leads to synthesis of abnormally long, poorly branched, and hyperphosphorylated glycogen that is insoluble and precipitates as polyglucosan Lafora bodies. These inclusions accumulate in neurones and other tissues, driving neuronal dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and progressive neurodegeneration that manifests as the characteristic progressive myoclonic epilepsy and dementia.
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of EPM2A and NHLRC1
EEG to document background slowing, generalised and occipital discharges, and photosensitivity
Skin biopsy for periodic acid-Schiff-positive Lafora bodies when genetics are inconclusive
Brain MRI to exclude structural causes and assess for atrophy
Metabolic and mitochondrial screening to exclude other progressive myoclonic epilepsies
redFlags: Rapidly worsening myoclonus and seizures becoming refractory to treatment
Progressive dementia and loss of independence in a previously healthy teenager
Aspiration, immobility, or status epilepticus signalling advanced disease
Deterioration after introduction of sodium-channel-blocking antiseizure drugs
reference.prognosis: Lafora disease is relentlessly progressive, with escalating myoclonus, refractory seizures, and dementia leading to profound disability and death typically within about a decade of onset.
pitfalls: Confusing Lafora disease with the more treatable Unverricht-Lundborg disease, giving falsely reassuring prognosis
Prescribing sodium-channel-blocking agents that aggravate myoclonus
Attributing early cognitive decline to psychiatric illness or medication
Delaying genetic confirmation and counselling in a suspected progressive myoclonic epilepsy
references: GeneReviews: Progressive Myoclonus Epilepsy, Lafora Type
management: Treat symptomatically with antiseizure medications effective against myoclonus and generalised seizures, such as valproate, levetiracetam, clonazepam and add-on perampanel, brivaracetam or zonisamide
Avoid sodium-channel-blocking agents such as phenytoin, carbamazepine and lamotrigine, which typically aggravate the myoclonus
Manage acute seizure clusters and status epilepticus with benzodiazepine rescue therapy and an emergency seizure plan
Provide supportive care for progressive disability including physiotherapy, nutritional support and gastrostomy feeding for dysphagia
Coordinate multidisciplinary and palliative input across neurology, dietetics, psychology and community services
Offer genetic counselling and testing of at-risk relatives given autosomal recessive inheritance
Plan proactively for advancing dementia and dependency, escalating to end-of-life care as the disease progresses
